pathophysiology.summary: Nausea and vomiting in advanced illness usually has an identifiable cause — drugs, metabolic disturbance, gastric stasis, bowel obstruction, raised intracranial pressure or anxiety. The cause predicts the pathway involved (chemoreceptor trigger zone, gut, vestibular, cortical) and therefore the antiemetic.
keyMechanisms: Chemical causes (opioids, hypercalcaemia, renal failure, infection, toxins) act on the chemoreceptor trigger zone via dopamine D2 — haloperidol is first line (MOH).
Gastric stasis or functional obstruction (tumour, ascites, hepatomegaly, opioids, anticholinergics) — prokinetic metoclopramide or domperidone (MOH).
Raised intracranial pressure and vestibular causes act via histamine H1/muscarinic pathways — cyclizine, with steroids for raised ICP (MOH).
Visceral damage from tumour or radiotherapy releases serotonin — ondansetron with or without corticosteroids (MOH).
Anxiety and anticipation act via the cortex — non-drug measures, then benzodiazepine or levomepromazine (MOH).

symptoms: Persistent nausea unrelieved by vomiting (chemical cause).
Fullness, regurgitation, large-volume undigested vomit relieved by vomiting (gastric stasis).
Headache, visual disturbance, worse with movement (raised ICP/vestibular); anticipatory nausea (anxiety).
physicalSigns: Dehydration; abdominal distension, succussion splash, hepatomegaly, ascites.
Bowel sounds absent or tinkling, colic (obstruction).
Papilloedema, focal neurology (raised ICP); oral candidiasis.
redFlags: Faeculent vomiting, colic, distension, no flatus — bowel obstruction
Headache with vomiting and neurology — raised intracranial pressure
Extrapyramidal reaction to metoclopramide or haloperidol

differentials.distinguishingFeatures: Colic, distension, absent flatus — see Malignant Bowel Obstruction topic.
Temporal link to a new drug or dose.
Epigastric pain, NSAID or steroid use.

ruleIn.modalityTarget: When a metabolic cause is possible and results would change care
ruleIn.clinicalRationale: Metabolic cause → haloperidol; review renally cleared drugs (MOH).

clinicalManagement.title: Find the cause
actions: Assess pattern of nausea and vomiting, drugs, bowels, calcium/renal function and neurology (NICE NG31 1.5.18).
Treat reversible causes: constipation, hypercalcaemia, infection, offending drugs.
Choose the antiemetic by mechanism; consider non-drug measures (NICE NG31 1.5.20).

clinicalManagement.title: First antiemetic by cause (MOH Protocol-010)
actions: Chemical/metabolic/drug: haloperidol 0.5–3 mg PO/SC at night, or 0.5–3 mg/24 h by syringe driver (maximum 5 mg); alternative levomepromazine 6.25–25 mg at night.
Gastric stasis/functional obstruction: metoclopramide 10 mg PO/SC three to four times daily, or 30–40 mg/24 h by syringe driver; or domperidone 10 mg PO three times daily (QT risk).
Raised ICP/vestibular: cyclizine 50 mg PO/SC three times daily, or 150 mg/24 h by syringe driver; consider steroids.
Visceral/radiotherapy damage: ondansetron 4–8 mg PO/SC two to three times daily, or 16 mg/24 h by syringe driver; with or without corticosteroids.
Anxiety: non-drug measures first, then a benzodiazepine, then levomepromazine.

clinicalManagement.title: Refractory nausea
actions: Dexamethasone 8–16 mg daily for refractory nausea and vomiting (MOH Protocol-010 p. 4).
Use a subcutaneous syringe driver if oral absorption is unreliable or more than 2–3 PRN doses are needed in 24 h (NICE NG31 1.5.6).

regimens.indication: Chemical, metabolic or drug-related nausea (first line)
regimens.dose: 0.5–3 mg (syringe driver 0.5–3 mg/24 h, maximum 5 mg)
contraindications: Severe toxic CNS depression or coma

learningObjectives: Identify the cause of nausea and vomiting in advanced illness and choose a mechanism-based antiemetic.
pitfalls: Metoclopramide with colic or complete obstruction.
keyPoints: Treat the cause, then pick the antiemetic by mechanism.
Metoclopramide for stasis — not in complete obstruction.
Syringe driver if more than 2–3 PRN doses/day.

patientEducation: Small frequent meals; avoid strong smells.
Report colic, vomiting faeculent material, headache.
lifestyleAndDiet: Small, frequent, bland meals; oral hygiene.
dischargeCriteria: Symptoms controlled for the chosen place of care, or safe transfer arranged.
Patient and family know the plan, the medicines and whom to call.
nonClinicalManagement.followUpPlan: Review antiemetic response at least daily until controlled; reassess the cause if the pattern changes.
